lead: A car needs more than one kind of bus. A door switch sends a few bits now and then; steering and damping need messages at exactly known times; cameras and maps need very high bandwidth. LIN (Local Interconnect Network) is a cheap single-wire master-slave bus for body switches and motors. FlexRay is a dual-channel, time-triggered bus for chassis and x-by-wire control. Automotive Ethernet is a switched, single-pair network for cameras, infotainment and the backbone. This chapter shows how each one works, with frame timing and rates you can calculate, and where each fits beside CAN.
prereq: You need CAN and CAN FD for the comparison, and the bus classes from topology, OSI model and classification.

blocks.text: LIN links small body modules: window lifters, mirrors, seat motors and climate flaps. It uses one signal wire plus ground, at battery voltage: the master has a 1 kΩ pull-up resistor and each slave about 30 kΩ, and a node pulls the wire low for a dominant 0. A cluster has one master (usually a body ECU that is also on CAN) and up to 15 slaves, at 1 to 20 kbit/s; 19.2 kbit/s is common.

The master owns a schedule table, a fixed list of frames and the time slot for each. For every slot it sends a header; the one node that publishes that frame (a slave, or the master itself) sends the response, and any node that needs the data reads it. Only the master starts frames, so there are no collisions and the timing is known.

items: Break: at least 13 dominant bits and a recessive delimiter. It marks the start of a frame, so every slave knows a header is coming. (Waking a sleeping cluster is a separate wake-up pulse.)
Sync: the byte 0x55 (alternating bits), from which slaves measure the bit time.
Protected identifier (PID): a 6-bit frame identifier (0 to 63) plus 2 parity bits, P0 = ID0 ⊕ ID1 ⊕ ID2 ⊕ ID4 and P1 = NOT(ID1 ⊕ ID3 ⊕ ID4 ⊕ ID5). It names the frame, not a slave.
Checksum: the classic checksum covers the data bytes; the enhanced checksum (LIN 2.x) covers the PID as well. Diagnostic frames 0x3C and 0x3D always use the classic one.

blocks.where: T is the nominal frame time; 34 bits is the nominal header (break and delimiter 14, sync 10, PID 10); every byte on the wire takes 10 bits (start bit, 8 data bits, stop bit); n data bytes plus 1 checksum byte make the response; τ is one bit time (1 ÷ bit rate).
Tₘₐₓ is the longest time the frame may take; the 40 per cent margin allows for gaps between bytes. The schedule slot must be at least Tₘₐₓ.

sections.h3: FlexRay: fixed slots on two channels

blocks.text: FlexRay is for systems where a late message is itself a fault: active suspension, chassis control, brake-by-wire and steer-by-wire. It has two independent channels, A and B, each at up to 10 Mbit/s. A node may send the same frame on both channels for redundancy or different frames to double the rate. The wiring can be a passive bus, an active star (a star coupler that cuts off a faulty branch) or a mix.
Time is divided into repeating communication cycles, typically 1 to 5 ms long and numbered 0 to 63. Every node keeps a synchronised clock. Each cycle has four parts:

items: Static segment: time-division multiple access (TDMA). Equal slots, each owned by one node, repeat in the same order every cycle. No arbitration and no collisions, so the worst-case delay of a static message is one cycle.

Dynamic segment: flexible TDMA (FTDMA) on minislots. A slot counter steps through the minislots; a node whose turn comes and has data starts its frame and stretches its slot to the frame length, which leaves less time for later numbers. A node with nothing to send uses just one short minislot. Low numbers therefore have priority.

Symbol window: carries short symbols such as the collision avoidance symbol (CAS) and the media access test symbol (MTS). Start-up frames travel in static slots, and wake-up uses its own wake-up pattern.
Network idle time (NIT): no traffic; nodes correct their clocks.

blocks.text: A FlexRay frame has a 5-byte header (frame ID equal to the slot number, payload length, header CRC, cycle count), 0 to 254 payload bytes and a 24-bit CRC.

Office Ethernet uses two pairs (100BASE-TX) or four pairs (1000BASE-T) and heavy connectors. Automotive Ethernet sends full duplex over one unshielded twisted pair: 100BASE-T1 at 100 Mbit/s and 1000BASE-T1 at 1 Gbit/s, using echo cancellation so both ends can talk at once. Each link joins exactly two devices, so the network is a star of switches with no collisions. A switch forwards a frame only to the port that leads to its destination, so many transfers run in parallel. 10BASE-T1S (10 Mbit/s) is the exception: several nodes can share one short multidrop pair, which suits zonal links that used to be CAN.

Ethernet carries camera and radar streams, infotainment, software downloads and the backbone. VLAN tags keep safety, body and infotainment traffic apart on one switch. Above IP, SOME/IP (scalable service-oriented middleware over IP) lets an ECU call a service by name, and DoIP (diagnostics over IP) speeds up flashing. Plain Ethernet is not deterministic; AVB/TSN (audio video bridging, time-sensitive networking) adds clock synchronisation and scheduled traffic for bounded latency.

examples.question: A LIN window-lifter slave sends a response of 8 data bytes at 19.2 kbit/s. (a) Find the nominal and maximum frame times. (b) The master's schedule has five frames, each given a 10 ms slot. Is 10 ms long enough for this frame, and how often is each frame sent?
steps: Bits on the wire: header 34 + response 10 × (8 + 1) = 34 + 90 = 124 bits.
Nominal frame time: 124 × 52.08 µs = 6458 µs = 6.46 ms.
9.04 ms is less than the 10 ms slot, so the slot is long enough.
Schedule cycle: 5 slots × 10 ms = 50 ms, so each frame is sent every 50 ms, 20 times a second.
examples.answer: Nominal 6.46 ms, maximum 9.04 ms; a 10 ms slot fits, and each of the five frames repeats every 50 ms.

examples.question: A 1000-byte block (a camera thumbnail, say) must cross the car. Ignoring protocol overhead, how long does it take on 19.2 kbit/s LIN, 500 kbit/s CAN, one 10 Mbit/s FlexRay channel and 100 Mbit/s Ethernet?
steps: Ratio LIN to Ethernet: 416.7 ms ÷ 0.08 ms ≈ 5208.
examples.answer: 416.7 ms on LIN, 16 ms on CAN, 0.8 ms on FlexRay and 80 µs on Ethernet; real times are longer because of headers, stuffing and gaps, but the ratio of about 5000 between LIN and Ethernet stands.

traps: LIN is not multi-master: only the master sends headers. A slave sends only a response, and only for the frame identifiers it publishes.
The LIN header names a frame, not a slave. One frame can be read by many nodes, and the master can publish a frame itself.
FlexRay is not purely event-driven: the static segment is TDMA and gives the guarantee; only the dynamic segment is FTDMA.
Automotive Ethernet uses one pair, not the two pairs of 100BASE-TX or the four of 1000BASE-T. In a LIN frame time every byte is 10 bits, and the checksum byte counts too.

quiz.q: State the maximum number of LIN slaves under one master and LIN's bit-rate range.
quiz.a: Up to 15 slaves under one master; 1 to 20 kbit/s, often 19.2 kbit/s.

quiz.q: Why does LIN use a schedule table instead of arbitration?
quiz.a: The master starts every frame in a fixed order, so frames cannot collide, slaves need no arbitration hardware and each frame's repeat time is known.

quiz.q: Find the protected identifier for LIN frame ID 0x3D.
A LIN frame with 2 data bytes runs at 19.2 kbit/s. Find its nominal and maximum times.
In the FlexRay dynamic segment, why do low slot numbers have priority?
quiz.a: The slot counter steps through the minislots in order. A node that sends stretches its slot, using up dynamic-segment time, so a high-numbered node may find no time left in this cycle.

quiz.q: A steer-by-wire signal must arrive within 5 ms. Compare CAN and FlexRay for it.
quiz.a: On CAN a frame can wait behind higher-priority frames and repeated error frames, so its worst case depends on bus load and faults. On FlexRay, a static slot in a 5 ms cycle (or shorter) arrives once every cycle on both channels, so the 5 ms bound is guaranteed and one broken channel is survived. FlexRay fits.

quiz.q: Why use 10BASE-T1S rather than 100BASE-T1 for a cluster of small door nodes?
quiz.a: 10BASE-T1S lets several nodes share one short pair, so no switch port per node is needed, and 10 Mbit/s is plenty for doors. 100BASE-T1 is point to point and needs a switch port for every node, which costs more.

beyond: Not for the exam. The industry is moving to a zonal layout: a few zone controllers near groups of sensors, joined by a gigabit Ethernet backbone with TSN, while LIN and CAN stay at the edges. Search for IEEE 802.1AS time sync, TSN scheduled traffic and 10BASE-T1S PLCA.
